issues.legal_issue: The medical evidence was consistent with the account that the deceased had been repeatedly crushed by a vehicle.
material_facts: The post-mortem findings included extensive injuries to the skull and left side of the chest, broken bones, and damage to internal organs.
The doctor testified that the injuries were possible from crushing by a tractor.
The spot panchnama recorded circular or round tyre marks.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was incorrect to treat the medical evidence as contradicting the prosecution account of repeated crushing.
issues.legal_principle: Medical evidence must be assessed alongside the injuries recorded at post-mortem, the doctor's testimony, and physical evidence at the scene. Here, those circumstances supported rather than belied the eyewitness account.

predicates.murder_prosecution: The proceeding concerned a prosecution for murder.
predicates.medical_findings_support_vehicle_crushin: The medical examiner recorded injuries capable of being caused by a vehicle crushing a person.
predicates.scene_marks_support_repeated_passes: Investigators found vehicle marks at the scene indicating repeated passes.

issues.definition: When a murder prosecution has medical findings supporting vehicle crushing and scene marks supporting repeated passes, the medical evidence is consistent with the prosecution account.

issues.legal_issue: A sole eyewitness's testimony may be relied on despite non-core improvements when the witness's presence is natural and the account is corroborated on material particulars.
material_facts: The sole eyewitness was accompanying a very elderly man whom he lived with and who depended on the household for assistance.
The eyewitness promptly reported the incident, and his account was supported by the scene evidence, the inquest, and the medical findings.
The eyewitness made some improvements concerning the exhortation and another person's presence, but those matters did not affect the core account.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness was natural, completely trustworthy, and could be relied on despite the improvements.
issues.legal_principle: A conviction may rest on a single witness if the court finds the testimony trustworthy and corroborated on material particulars: Ramnaresh v. State of Chhattisgarh (2012) 4 SCC 257, relying on Joseph v. State of Kerala (2003) 1 SCC 465 and State of Haryana v. Inder Singh (2002) 9 SCC 537. An FIR need not contain every detail, and non-fundamental improvements may be separated from the reliable substance of the testimony.

rule.if: criminal_trial and sole_witness_natural_presence and account_corroborated_on_material_particulars and improvements_do_not_affect_core_account

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding was a criminal trial concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.sole_witness_natural_presence: The sole eyewitness was naturally present at the relevant place and time because of the circumstances of the relationship and events.
predicates.account_corroborated_on_material_particu: Other evidence in the record supported the eyewitness's account on material particulars.
predicates.improvements_do_not_affect_core_account: The eyewitness made changes or additions that did not undermine the basic substance of the account.

issues.definition: When a sole eyewitness was naturally present, the account is corroborated on material particulars, and improvements do not affect its core, the testimony may support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reconsider an acquittal when the view supporting it is not a reasonably possible view of the evidence.
material_facts: The High Court acquitted the accused after finding the medical evidence inconsistent with the prosecution account and treating aspects of the eyewitness's testimony as unreliable.
The Supreme Court found that the medical and scene evidence supported the account and that the identified inconsistencies did not undermine its core.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's view was not a possible view, so the Supreme Court was entitled to consider the matter afresh.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, an appellate court should not interfere if the view taken is a possible one; where it is not a possible view, the appellate court may reconsider the matter afresh. The Court relied on Ramesh Babulal Doshi v. State of Gujarat (1996) 9 SCC 225.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_view_not_reasonably_possible: The appellate court found that the view on which the acquittal rested could not reasonably be sustained on the evidence.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, if the view supporting acquittal is not reasonably possible, the appellate court may reassess the matter.

issues.legal_issue: Where the evidence attributed the acts of exhortation and driving to two accused but did not establish the culpability of the other occupants, the latter were entitled to the benefit of doubt.
material_facts: The original report attributed the exhortation to one accused and the driving of the vehicle to another.
The other two accused were occupants of the vehicle but had no overt act attributed to them in the original report.
There was no material establishing that the other occupants had participated in a deliberate plan to kill the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal of the two occupants was affirmed, while the convictions of the accused identified as exhorting and driving were restored under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement that criminal culpability be established by the evidence, and gave the benefit of doubt where the record did not establish the other occupants' participation. The convictions restored against the two identified participants were under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and other_occupants_present and no_overt_act_attributed_to_occupants and no_material_establishes_their_participation

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding was an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.other_occupants_present: The persons whose culpability was in issue were present as occupants of the vehicle used in the attack.
predicates.no_overt_act_attributed_to_occupants: The evidence did not attribute a specific overt act to those occupants.
predicates.no_material_establishes_their_participat: The record contained no material establishing that those occupants participated in the criminal plan.

issues.definition: When occupants are present but no overt act or other material establishes their participation, they receive the benefit of doubt in an appeal against acquittal.

issues.legal_issue: Life imprisonment, rather than the death sentence imposed at trial, was the appropriate sentence for the murder convictions upheld on appeal.
material_facts: The trial court imposed the death sentence for the murder of a 90-year-old victim.
The Supreme Court restored the murder convictions of two accused but expressly declined to restore the death sentence.
issues.conclusion: The two convicted accused were sentenced to imprisonment for life.
issues.legal_principle: After restoring the convictions under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC, the Court determined that life imprisonment was the appropriate sentence and did not restore the death sentence.

predicates.murder_conviction_upheld: The final appellate court upheld a conviction for murder.
predicates.capital_sentence_under_review: A death sentence imposed in the case was before the appellate court for consideration.
predicates.victim_was_very_old: The person who was killed was of very advanced age.

issues.definition: When a murder conviction is upheld, a death sentence is under review, and the victim was very old, the court imposed life imprisonment in this case.
